Surviving Corporate Ep 2: Corporate stress isn't just burning you out. It's ageing your face.

Here's the biology 🧬:

Chronic stress breaks down collagen -> The protein keeping your skin firm and your under-eyes from looking like you just survived another Q4 close 😮‍💨

Why your under-eyes go first -> The skin there is the thinnest on your face. Add poor sleep, Thirsty Thursdays and team drinks into the mix and your body quietly stops prioritising skin repair. It switches into survival mode instead. And look, I'm not telling you to skip the drinks and I won’t be anytime soon. Corporate life is social and that matters. But knowing what's happening under the surface means you can work with your body, not against it 🍻

In a stressful corporate environment, your skin is fighting a daily battle. Here's what I personally do to slow the damage 🛡️

☕ Caffeinated Eye Cream Caffeine is a vasoconstrictor. It physically tightens blood vessels under the eye, reducing the pooling that causes dark circles and puffiness. Applied in the morning it firms the area and over time helps reduce chronic inflammation that accelerates skin ageing.

🌞 SPF Daily (No Exceptions) UV exposure breaks down collagen and elastin independently of anything else going on in your life. Your skin is already under pressure from a demanding job and broken sleep. SPF is the simplest thing you can add to your morning that directly slows visible ageing. No cream repairs ageing damage as well as preventing it.

⏰ No Caffeine After 2pm Caffeine has a half life of around 5 to 7 hours. A 3pm coffee is still 50% active in your system at 8 to 10pm. Poor sleep amplifies your stress response the next morning, which breaks down more collagen, which worsens under-eye ageing. Cutting caffeine early protects your overnight repair cycle, which is when most skin regeneration actually happens.

🚶 When stressed - Take a 5 Minute Walk During the Day. Even a short walk lowers stress, improves circulation and triggers endorphin release. Better circulation means more oxygen and nutrients reaching skin cells. Less stress means your body stays in repair mode longer throughout the day.

🫁 Double Inhale, Slow Exhale (If You Can't Leave Your Desk) Double inhale through the nose, slow exhale through the mouth. Repeat 5 times. Studies show this activates the parasympathetic nervous system within minutes, measurably reducing stress markers. When stress drops, your body switches back to repair and regeneration. Takes 60 seconds. Works.

🌙 Consider introducing a Retinol - it is a vitamin A derivative that directly stimulates collagen production at a cellular level, the exact collagen that chronic stress is breaking down. It also accelerates skin cell turnover, reducing the appearance of dark circles and fine lines over time. Start low (0.025 to 0.05%), use only at night, and always follow with SPF the next morning. One of the most clinically backed ingredients available in the world.

⚠️ Start once a week only. Your skin needs time to adjust to this active ingredient. Using it too often too soon will cause redness and irritation. Low percentage, low frequency, then build up slowly over weeks.

Save this for when your under eyes start doing more overtime than you do 😅

subtitles: Let me guess. You work in London and it's Thirsty Thursday, but you also need to be a functioning member of society before 8:00am. Welcome back to surviving corporate. Let's talk about the best pre night protocol to reduce that hangover. Two to three hours before you even think about crushing drinks, eat some food. Basic, but I don't see enough people doing this. Not a sandwich and actual meal. I'd recommend not sponsored. A farmer's days or a salad project. High protein, healthy fat. This will ensure alcohol absorption into your bloodstream is more gradual and your liver isn't taking the immediate hit. Now, to know none of this is gonna make your night less fun. It's just gonna mean you're not completely cook tomorrow. Second tip, get yourself electrolyte tablet. Best believe I'm having one before my first part. This is your liquidity buffer. Alcohol suppresses vasopressin, the hormone that tells your kidneys to retain water. You're going to lose sodium, potassium and magnesium all night through urine, starting with electrolytes already on board. Means your body has a reserve before the deficit even begin. And finally, which is something I'm terrible at doing myself. So try and drink some water during the night. Will it make you less drunk? No. The water does nothing for tonight, but everything for tomorrow's hangover. Simply when it's your round, just go to the bar, ask for a tap water, slam it. caption:
The Quirks of Natural Gas Futures!⛽️

Natural gas futures carry a well-known distortion around the March–April transition because it marks a hard shift from winter withdrawal season to spring injection season. March, the last winter contract, carries significant end-of-season storage risk, meaning prices can spike or collapse based on late-season cold or inventory tightness, while April reflects much softer, “shoulder-season” demand. This creates the infamous March–April spread—often called the widowmaker—where small weather forecast changes can produce outsized, nonlinear moves.

Did you know about this? Let me know in the comments and follow for more trading tidbits! 

#quantfinance #finance #optionstrading #stocks
subtitles: Why do March natural gas futures cover April, but April doesn't cover March? It's more intuitive than you think. Most beginner traders think that hedging works both ways for natural gas, but it doesn't. The difference comes down to seasonal demand risk. March is the tail end of winter and April is a shoulder month. In March, heating demand is still high, but in April, heating demand drops off. A cold snap in April is less likely and less severe. This is what makes March riskier than April. March trades at a premium to April. This is what's known as backwardation. That premium reflects the winter tail risk. When you buy March, you're buying insurance against a late season cold snap. But when you're buying April, you're not buying that insurance. You're exposed to March spikes. That's why March covers April, but April doesn't cover March. The March April spread is notorious in the industry. They call it the widowmaker because of how volatile it is. As winter progresses, the spread can narrow or flip, but the risk of a sudden severe cold still remains higher in March than in April. This makes March the robust insurance policy against volatility. This is how professionals think about energy hedging. They understand seasonal risk and how real life events can affect pricing. That's the instrument that blew up during the 2008 financial crisis. Banks like JP Morgan and Goldman Sachs are the biggest swap dealers in the world. Hedge funds use them to take massive leverage positions. And even airlines use them to lock in fuel prices so that a spike in oil prices doesn't destroy their margins. So why does this even matter? That's what makes this such a great place to visit with friends, because everyone knows us girlies always have a hard time deciding on one place to eat. The second truck we tried is called Hard Pressed and they are known for their nashburgers, beef tallow fries, and hard sauce. All burgers are served on a King's Hawaiian bun. I Personally judge a burger by its bun and you will always win me over if you're using a King's Hawaiian. This was another wonderful date night and we will be back for that dino rib burrito. And maybe I'll be crazy and try the Hard Press Triple burger. Comment if you think I can finish either. El Camino is open every day of the week until midnight and 2:00am on Fridays and Saturdays. We didn't want it to be too serious. We're just having fun here. And like I said, today we are at Commonwealth Coffee off of Broadway, close to U I W. I am an avid reader, and I started a book club at work back in 2,024. I quickly Learned that I had other co workers who enjoy reading in their past time. Our goal is to read 12 books per year, with one person being randomly selected to pick our next read. That became a little too daunting, and it started to feel like we were doing book reports for school, so Book Club took a hiatus for the year of 2025. But we are back and stronger than ever in 2026. And this year we're doing things a little bit different. Our new goal is to read six books per year, and we will meet every other month as a group. We have decided on six different genres we want to explore this year. We let the Google Wheel of names side the genre for us, and then we look at books that fall within that genre. Each member will then submit their book suggestion in our group chat. Then each person votes on which book they would want to read. The top three books with the most Votes will get put into the Google Wheel of names, and our next read lies in the fate of the Google Wheel. This method is working for us and I can't wait to share more of our book club shenanigans, so be sure to follow along!

subtitles: If you can answer these four questions about your finances, you are already ahead of 90% of people. Starting with question No. 1 what's your gross first net pay? Most people, me included, at 1.2, only know the amount that's hitting your bank account every month. But understanding your taxes and then your pre tax deduction like your retirement, your health insurance can help you optimize your W4, but also just reduce your taxable income overall. Question No. 2 what are your total debt balances and their interest rates? Having $10,000 worth of student loans at 3% is so much different than having $10,000 worth of credit card debt at 22%. When you know your numbers, you can pay down your debt strategically instead of just throwing money at whatever feels urgent. Or if you are in the situation where you have student loans at 3%, it may make more sense to invest your money instead of paying down your debt. Moving on to question No. 3 what percentage of your income are you saving and investing? This is important for obvious reasons, but instead of just randomly saving whatever money you have left over, it's really helpful to have a set percentage and to pay yourself first and and to even automate it. That's your thing so you don't even have to think about it. And our last question how much money do you spend each month and on what categories? I feel like most people wildly underestimate how Much money they spend. I know I used to do that. Once you start paying attention to how much money is going out the door, you can notice patterns. And you can also just create awareness so that you can start spending your money in a way that's more intentional or more aligned with your values.

Your journey to financial freedom won’t be easy but these are the 4 stages we all go through on your journey. Know you’re not alone!
#personalfinance #financialfreedom #financetok #moneymanagement #selfimprovement
subtitles: Alright, over the past 12 months, I have changed the entire financial trajectory of my life. From 12 months ago, not even knowing what career I wanted to pursue, to now moving into the process of buying my first home. Life can change fast. And as someone who's experienced this, these are the 4 stages you'll go through on your journey to financial freedom. And let's start off with number one, education. This usually comes in the form of inspiration that's external, whether it's a book like how to think and grow Rich, or you watch your favourite personal finance creators like Mia Ray or me. This is the stage where you learn all about money, how it works, saving, investing, business, debt, and the list honestly goes on. And once you feel like you've learnt enough, then you move on to stage 2, which is addiction. Now, this is the stage where you become hyper addicted to reaching your financial goals. Whether it's paying off debt or investing into the stock market. You spend every single waking hour working towards that goal. And next you have stage 3, which I think is the most crucial, but most people are too scared to talk about it, and it's nihilism at this point You've been working towards your financial goals for a while now, and you may have even made that cannon event bad financial decision. Maybe you invested into the wrong stocks or crypto, you overspent, maybe even moved out. Of your parents home too early. And now it feels like your financial goals are so far out of reach that you kind of wanna give up. You sit there thinking, what's the point in all of this? But I promise you, once you make it through the storm, you make it to the last stage, which is acceptance. Now this is the stage where you're able to find a sweet balance between your financial goals and enjoying life. And you're able to build a well structured plan around that vision. This is exactly how I was able to save for a house deposit in six months. And I've known many people who are able to build a structured plan to retire early. subtitles: Imagine you just bought a new laptop for $1,200. You put it on your credit card for the cash back and purchase Protection. Smart move. The money is already sitting in your checking account. You wait for the statement. You see the charge and you pay every single cent before the due date. No interest, no late fees, textbook responsible behavior. Then two days later, you open your credit monitoring app and your stomach drops. Your score fell 30 points overnight. No mispayments, no new accounts, no fraud, just a mysterious nose dive that nobody warned you about. If this has happened to you, you are not alone. Millions of Americans watch their credit scores swing wildly every month and they have absolutely no idea why, because nobody ever taught them the one calendar date that actually controls their score. It is not the due date. It is a completely different date that your bank buries in the fine print. In this video, I'm going to break down exactly how your bank photographs your financial life, why that photograph almost always catches you at your worst and how shifting one payment by just two days can separate a decent score from an elite one. Today, we are cracking open credit utilization, the most misunderstood and most powerful variable in the entire credit scoring formula. Payment history takes a decade to build. A hard inquiry sits on your report for two full years, but utilization resets like a light switch. The Moment, you understand the reporting calendar. We are going to cover exactly when your bank sends your data to the credit bureaus. Why paying in full does not mean your report looks clean and the exact percentage targets that separate good from phenomenal. If this kind of content helps you see through the smoke and mirrors of modern finance, subscribe. That single click keeps this channel alive. Now let us talk about the trap. From a young age, we are conditioned to worship the payment due date and it matters. Miss it and you get a late fee and a negative Mark that follows you for 7 years. But here is the problem. We assume that when we send a payment, the credit bureaus, Experian, Transunion and Equifax update instantly like a live scoreboard. That is a fantasy. The credit reporting system does not work like a video stream. It works like a security camera that takes one still image per month and the timing of that image has nothing to do with when you pay. For most people, the camera clicks on the worst possible day, when your balance is at its peak, weeks before you actually pay it off. Here is the anatomy of a billing cycle. Say your cycle runs from the 5th to the 4th of the next month. Every swipe adds to your running balance. On the 4th, the cycle closes. Your bank locks in that balance, generates a statement and this moment, the statement Closing date is the single most important date in your credit life. Whatever balance appears on that statement is the exact number your bank sends to the bureaus. It gets stamped onto your report for the entire month, but your payment is not due until roughly 21 to 25 days later. So if $2,500 was on your card when the statement cut, that $2,500 gets reported even if you pay it all off two weeks later. You paid zero interest, you slept soundly, but on your credit report, it looks like you owe $2,500. The fix is simple. Instead of paying after the statement arrives, you pay before the statement is generated. You find your statement closing date and three to four days before it hits, you push a payment that drops your balance to almost nothing. When the cycle closes, the bank sees a tiny balance and that tiny number is what gets reported. Same spending habits, same total amount paid, completely different credit report. Now let me show you why this matters so much. The Fico model breaks your score into 5 categories. Payment history is the biggest at 35%, but sitting right behind it at 30% is amounts owed, which is almost entirely driven by credit utilization. Nearly one third of your financial reputation depends on how much credit you are using at the exact moment the bank takes its snapshot. It outweighs the length of your credit history. It outweighs your mix of credit types. You Could have 15 years of flawless payments. But if utilization spikes for one month, that 30% slice collapses and drags your score with it. The math is simple. Division balance divided by limit. If you owe 600 dollars on a 2 thousand dollar card, you are at 30% and that is exactly where the first cliff begins. Below 10%, you are golden. Between 10 and 30, you are fine. Cross 30%, the algorithm flags you as a risk. Cross 50, you look like a crisis push. Near 100 and your score goes into freefall. And this applies both to your overall utilization across all cards and to each individual card. You could have 40 thousand dollars in total credit, but if one card with a 2,500 dollar limit is maxed out, the algorithm treats that single card as a red flag. But here is the silver lining. Unlike a missed payment that haunts you for seven years, utilization has zero memory. The Fico 8 model only cares about your most recent reported balance. If you were at 85% last month and tanked, but this month you report 4%, your score bounces back as if the 85% never existed. One good snapshot erases the last bad one. Now you might think the goal is zero utilization on every card. If low is good, zero must be perfect, right? Wrong. Reporting zero across every card can actually produce a lower score than reporting a small balance. The Fico model evaluates how you Manage debt. If every card shows zero month after month, the model has no evidence you are actively using credit. You look inactive. And an inactive borrower is a slightly bigger question Mark than someone who uses credit responsibly. People with perfect 850 scores tend to hover between 1 and 7% utilization. The optimal strategy is called all card zero except one. Pay every card to zero before their statement dates, but on one card, leave a tiny balance, maybe $10 or 1% of the limit. This tells the algorithm you are using credit but keeping it extremely low. And here is the key distinction. Reporting a balance is not the same as carrying a balance. You report $10 when the statement closes, then pay that $10 before the due date three weeks later. Zero interest maximum score. Here is the execution plan. Step 1, find the statement closing date for every card. This is not the due date. Open a past statement PDF and look for billing cycle ends or statement closing date. Put these dates in your calendar with a reminder 2 to three days before. Step 2, on your reminder day, check your balance. If it is $1,400 and you want to report about $50, manually push a payment of $1,350 right then. Do not wait for auto pay. Step 3, verify the statement when it post. It should show your small target amount. Then make sure that amount gets paid by the actual due date. The First few times, double check manually. The worst outcome is getting clever with utilization and accidentally missing a payment. You do not need to do this every month. This level of precision really only matters when you are applying for something important in the next 60 days, a mortgage, auto loan or business line of credit. The rest of the year, keep utilization loosely under 20% and let auto pay handle it. One major warning, there is a line between smart timing and dangerous behavior called credit cycling. If you have a two thousand dollar limit and you spend 2 thousand dollars, pay it off, spend another 2 thousand dollars and pay it off again. In the same month, you have pushed 4 thousand dollars through a card approved for two thousand dollars. Banks interpret this as potential fraud or money laundering. They may freeze your account, demand tax returns or shut you down. Keep monthly spending within your limit. If you constantly hit your ceiling, do not gain the payments. Call and request a credit limit increase instead. One last defensive tip, do not close old unused credit cards. Your overall utilization is total balances divided by total available credit. Closing a card with an 8 thousand dollar limit removes 8 thousand dollars from your denominator. Your debt stays the same, but your utilization percentage spikes instantly. Keep old cards open, put a small recurring subscription on them, set auto pay and let them quietly pad your available credit Here is the full playbook. Find your statement closing date, calculate your utilization and aim for under 10%. Three days before the statement closes, pay down to about 1% of your limit. Let the statement generate and that tiny balance gets reported. Then pay off the remainder by the due date. Zero interest maximum score a two step payment rhythm that separates your real spending from your reported spending. Try this for one month. Pick your highest balance card, find the closing date, pay it down early and watch your monitoring app. When you see the jump, come back and tell me how many points you gained. caption:
You don’t need more motivation. You need fewer distractions and a system that makes focus easier.

1. Remove distractions before you even start:

Don’t rely on willpower mid-study. Put your phone in another room, log out of social media, and keep only the tabs you actually need. If distraction is not accessible, your brain won’t chase it.

2. Study in focused time blocks:
Instead of long, tiring sessions, use 45–50 minutes of deep focus followed by a 10-minute break. During that time, give full attention to one task only. No multitasking, no switching.

3. Define exactly what you’re going to do:
Saying “I’ll study chemistry” is too vague. Decide something like “revise polymers + solve 15 questions.” When your goal is clear, your brain stays engaged and less likely to wander.

4. Make your study space distraction proof:
Keep your desk clean and minimal. No unnecessary items, no noise, no visual clutter. A calm environment reduces mental chaos and helps you stay locked in longer.

5. Start small, but start immediately:
The hardest part is starting. Tell yourself you’ll study for just 5 minutes. Once you begin, resistance drops and focus builds naturally. Waiting for motivation only delays progress.

Distraction is not your personality. It’s just a habit you can rewire.

“I don’t know how to combine lifting and running”
Well… most don’t 🤷🏻‍♂️

Most who try to lift and run at the same time end up mediocre at both.

They either run so much they lose all their size and strength, or their lifts aren’t structured properly so they can barely jog a mile without their knees screaming or because of sore legs.

You do not have to choose between being strong and being fast. But you do need a system that builds both without one destroying the other.

This is how I structure a hybrid training week for my clients and for myself as someone who’s 220lbs lean, strong and fast:
✅ Monday - Upper Body Strength
✅ Tuesday - Speed or Tempo Run
✅ Wednesday - Lower Strength 
✅ Thursday - Easy Run (Zone 2)
✅ Friday - Upper Hypertrophy
✅ Saturday - Long Run
✅ Sunday - Full Rest

The key is intentional separation. 

Strength training is the priority in the gym with accessories for hypertrophy to get the “look”

Easy runs exist to build your aerobic base and burn more fat without trashing your recovery. 

Conditioning on lifting days build work capacity using Hyrox style movements like sled pushes, wall balls, and rower intervals so you are training for performance, not just aesthetics.

- 6 sessions. 
- No double days. 
- Fits a real schedule. 
- Builds a body that is strong, fast, lean, and built to perform.

caption:
I met Muko and her daughter Masani today.

Muko left Myanmar at 17, fleeing civil war. She built a new life here in Thailand. This is where she raised her daughter, and this is where she works. She weaves scarves by hand about 2 days for the smaller ones and up to 4 days for the larger pieces. Along with other hand man crafts. 

At first, I felt uncomfortable like I was at a zoo, staring at the latest captured animal. I know what it feels like to be seen as entertainment instead of a human being.

So I asked my guide first, then I asked her directly. She told me she welcomes it. Most people will never come here, and this is how they share their culture with the world.

Muko was wearing 27 rings. Masani was wearing 5. The rings don’t actually make the neck longer they slowly push the shoulders down over time, creating the illusion. Some say the tradition started as protection from tiger attacks. Others trace it back to their origin stories, tied to dragons and geese.

They usually begin wearing them around age five. Today, many daughters are given a choice. Most still choose to wear them, because they grow up seeing their mothers that way, and that becomes their standard of beauty.

- 2 large boneless, skinless chicken breasts (sliced horizontally into 4 thin cutlets)
Salt & freshly cracked black pepper
- ½ cup all-purpose flour (for dredging)
- 3–4 tbsp olive oil
- 3 tbsp unsalted butter (divided)
- 3 cloves garlic, minced
- ½ cup dry white wine (like Pinot Grigio or Sauvignon Blanc)
- 1 cup chicken broth
- ⅓ cup fresh lemon juice
- ¼ cup capers
- 2 tbsp fresh parsley, chopped
- Lemon slices (optional, for garnish)                                               Pat chicken dry.
Season both sides generously with salt and pepper.
Lightly dredge in flour, shaking off excess.
Heat olive oil and 1 tbsp butter in a large skillet over medium-high heat. Cook chicken 3–4 minutes per side until golden brown and cooked through.Transfer to a plate and tent loosely with foil.
In the same pan, reduce heat to medium.Add garlic and sauté 30 seconds (don’t let it brown).
Pour in white wine, scraping up brown bits. Simmer 2–3 minutes.
Add chicken broth and lemon juice. Let simmer 5 minutes until slightly reduced.
Stir in capers.
Whisk in remaining 2 tbsp butter until sauce is glossy.
Return chicken to the pan and simmer 2–3 minutes, spooning sauce over top.
Sprinkle with fresh parsley and add lemon slices.

subtitles: On this episode of Getting Financially Lit, we're talking DIRT. D. I. R. T. Stands for Deposit Interest Retention Tax in Ireland. It's the tax that's applied to the interest you earn on savings. In most cases it's taken automatically by your bank, so you never see the full amount. The current DIRT rate is 33%, so if your savings earns 100 euro in interest, you'll usually see about 67 euro. This isn't necessarily a penalty, and it doesn't mean that saving is pointless. Savings have a very specific job, safety, liquidity, and peace of mind. But between inflation and DIRT, savings aren't designed to build wealth over time. They're designed to protect money, not grow it. That's why people use different tools for different goals. Savings for security, investing for long term growth. Understanding DIRT isn't about trying to optimize every euro, it's about knowing how the system actually works so there's no surprises. And if you want to get financially literate in 2026, follow for more finance concepts explained simply.

subtitles: Okay, I want to explain why I've decided to invest in etfs in Ireland. Anyway, hear me out. The simplest way for ordinary people to invest in the market. Etfs are taxed harshly in Ireland. We know this. Exit tax, 8 year deemed disposal. Yes, that still matters. But investing isn't just about tax. It's about risk, diversification, behavior, and how likely your investment is to succeed in the long term. One of the key reasons etfs work is automatic rebalancing. In plain English, that means as markets move, some companies and sectors grow faster than others. Etfs automatically trim what's grown too large, top up what's lagged, and keeps your exposure spread across markets and sectors without you having to make those decisions. That's incredibly powerful and very hard to replicate consistently on your own. Yes, there are more tax efficient options available in Ireland. subtitles: Welcome back to Irish money reality finding your lost pensions part 2. So you found your old pension pots, well done. Now the real question is what do I actually do with them? If you change jobs a few times in Ireland, there's a good chance that you now have a few pension pots sitting with different providers. Once you've tracked them down, you have a couple of options. Before moving anything, it's worth checking these three things fees, fund options and access rules. Option 1 leave the pension pot where it is when you leave a job. That pension can usually stay in the scheme as what's called a preserved benefit. That simply means that you stop contributing. But the pension pot stays invested there until retirement. Leaving it where it is can make sense when some employer schemes actually have very competitive institutional pricing. The scheme offers strong fund options. You want to keep earlier access rules. Some occupational schemes may allow earlier access once you've left that employer, whereas consolidating it could mean accessing it later. Or sometimes it's simply a large pension pot that's working well and there's not really a strong reason to move it. The other option could be transferring that pension pot somewhere else. That might involve moving it to your current employer's pension scheme, if that scheme accepts transfers or a P R S A. Consolidating might make sense when the historical fees are actually higher than newer options. The scheme has Limited fund options or you simply want one place to manage everything long term. Consolidation isn't automatically better. Sometimes the best pension is the one you already have. subtitles: The Irish investing landscape is complicated and that's why most people never get started. Most of it comes down to just three pieces of the puzzle. 1. The investing vehicle. What you're investing through in Ireland. Your main options are pensions, individual shares, funds or property. The next question is how is it taxed? Because this is where outcomes really start to change. Pensions. You get tax relief going in and your investments grow tax free while invested. Your pension is one of the most tax efficient ways to invest in Ireland. When you draw it down, up to 200,000 euro is tax free. Everything after that up to 500,000 euro is tax at 20% and the rest is taxes income at the marginal rate. So you are tax later, but you get the benefit of all that compounding. First let's move on to shares or individual stocks. These fall under the capital gains tax system. 33% tax on gains when you sell, but make sure to make use of the 1,270 euro annual tax exemption. This system also applies to any company shares you might have received as part of your pay package through work. Let's move on to funds and etfs. These fall under the gross roll up tax system. This is where Arlene gets a bit unique. 38% exit tax on gains and crucially a forced deemed disposal tax event every eight years even if you don't choose to sell. And finally, property rental income is taxed As income at your marginal rate. If you sell the property, you pay 33% capital gains tax on that gain, unless it's your principal private residence. SO2 investments can perform the same, but what you actually keep can be very different. Once you understand and have chosen the investment vehicle and understand how it's taxed, there's one final piece of the puzzle that determines whether you actually build wealth or not. And that is time. In the market. This is what truly builds wealth. If your money stays invested, your returns start earning their own returns. That's compounding. Ireland has confirmed that it is going to push for something called the digital euro during our EU presidency starting in July. Most people hear digital euro and think, don't we already have that? I tap my card, money moves. What's new? Here's the difference. When you tap your card, that money flows through visa or Mastercard, American companies, then through your bank. The digital euro would be different. It would be actual central bank money, just in digital form. And just to be really clear, this is not cryptocurrency. No volatility, no speculation, no blockchain investing angle. It's still the euro, just issued digitally by the central bank. And when I say central bank, I mean the ECB, the European Central Bank, the institution behind the euro itself. So why should you care? Three reasons. 1. Sovereignty. Right now, nearly every digital payment you make in Ireland goes through American infrastructure. And in a world where trade wars and sanctions are becoming normal, that's a dependency. The digital euro is Europe saying we need our own rails. 2. It's public money, not private. The euros in your bank account. Technically, that's a claim on your bank. The digital euro would be a direct claim on the ECB, the same as physical cash. If your bank collapsed tomorrow, that digital euro is still yours. 3. Privacy. And this Is where it gets interesting. They're talking about cash like privacy for small, possibly offline payments. But this is also where most of the pushback is coming from, because on the other side of that, a fully digital state backed currency could mean more visibility over how money moves. Now, the ECB has said they're not trying to build a surveillance tool, but the reality is the rules here aren't fully locked in yet. And this is the part to watch. subtitles: Planning for your child's future and understanding inheritance rules actually go hand in hand, because how you build that money now affects how it's taxed and passed on later. Welcome back to Irish Money reality, where we discuss the weird, messy and uniquely Irish parts of our money system that no one ever really explains properly. If you want to build a pot of money for your child in Ireland for university, a house deposit, or just to pass on wealth, well, it's not as simple as it should be. In the UK you just open a junior stocks and shares ISA and Bob's your uncle. Simple, clean, tax free, up to £9,000 a year. In Ireland we don't have that. So instead you need to understand how the system works. This is part 1, where I'll break down the tax rules simply, and in Part 2, I'll break down the actual options available. There are really two tax rules that drive everything here. The first is the big lifetime limit. Over time, your child can receive up to 400,000 euro from their parents, combined in gifts and inheritance, before paying tax. That includes things like cash, property or investments that you pass on over time or at the end. After that, a 33% capital acquisition tax applies. Then separately, you can gift your child 3,000 euro per year per parent, completely tax free. And these are two separate things. That 3,000 euro does not reduce the 400,000 euro lifetime Limit, but only if you actually give it each year. You can't go back later and retroactively claim it. So if two parents use this properly, 6,000 euro a year is 108,000 euro after 18 years moved across without touching the 400,000 euro limit. So once you understand that you have to choose your trade offs, because in Ireland you don't get one simple tax free option. In part 2 I'll break down the actual options available. 🧠 9 hobbies that genuinely sharpen your mind

1. 📚 Deep reading
Not summaries. Not threads.
Books that make you stay with ideas longer than is comfortable — and stretch your focus.

2. ✍️ Writing to clarify thinking
Not for posting.
Journals, notes, rough drafts.
Putting thoughts on paper so they become clearer.

3. 🛠️ Building a high-leverage skill
Coding, design, editing, writing.
Skills that compound over time instead of expiring.

4. 🚶 Walking without stimulation
No music. No podcasts. No phone.
Just your thoughts and your surroundings.

5. ♟️ Playing strategy-based games
Chess, logic puzzles, long-term strategy games.
Training foresight and decision-making.

6. 🧩 Studying human behavior
Psychology, observation, pattern recognition.
Learning why people act the way they do.

7. 🧘‍♂️ Intentional movement
Strength training or yoga.
Using the body to sharpen the mind.

8. 👀 Practicing visual awareness
Studying design, architecture, film, or art.
Learning to notice structure, balance, and detail.

9. 🎓 Teaching what you’re learning
Explaining ideas to others — or even to yourself.
Nothing tests understanding better.

✨ Intelligence isn’t built by consuming more.
📈 It’s built by practicing better habits consistently.

📚 How to Stay Active & Focused While Studying

1️⃣ Study at the Right Time ⏰
🌅 Early morning hits different (4:30–7 AM = fresh brain).
🍛 Avoid heavy study right after lunch.
🛏️ And please… don’t study on your bed (Bed = sleep mode ON).

2️⃣ Fix Your Sitting Setup 🪑
✔️ Use a chair & table.
✔️ Keep your back straight.
💡 Bright light is a must.
📖 Books at eye level = less strain, more focus.

3️⃣ Refresh Yourself 💧
❄️ Wash your face with cold water.
🚰 Keep a water bottle near you.
🥤 Sip water often.
🍋 Lemon water = instant refresh.

4️⃣ Be Smart with Drinks ☕
☕ Tea/coffee is okay (but don’t overdo it).
🚫 Avoid sugary drinks.
🌙 No caffeine at night — protect your sleep cycle.

5️⃣ Follow the 25–5 Rule ⏳ (Pomodoro)
📖 25 minutes deep study.
🧘 5 minutes break.
🚶 Walk, stretch, breathe.
🔁 Repeat.
This keeps mental fatigue away.

6️⃣ 2-Minute Energy Boost ⚡
🏃 20 jumping jacks.
🚶 Fast walking in your room.
🤸 Stretch neck & hands.
🌬️ 5 deep breaths.

➡️ Move your body = activate your brain.

7️⃣ Eat Light 🍎
🚫 Avoid heavy rice meals, oily food & overeating.
🥜 Choose fruits, nuts & light snacks.

8️⃣ Sleep Properly 😴
🛌 6–8 hours sleep is non-negotiable.
❌ Don’t pull all-nighters daily.
⏱️ If needed, take a 20-minute power nap (not 2 hours).

9️⃣ Make Study Active ✍️
❌ Don’t just read.
📝 Write notes.
👨‍🏫 Teach an imaginary student.
🧠 Solve questions.
🖍️ Highlight & speak out loud.

➡️ Active study = less sleepiness.

🚨 Emergency Tip (Very Sleepy?)

🧍 Stand and study.
🔊 Read loudly.
🔄 Switch subjects.
🔥 Start with the toughest topic first.

💪 Discipline > Motivation
Fix your habits, and focus will follow 💯

The Fear and Greed Index is a tool used by investors to measure the emotional sentiment of the stock market. It helps determine whether investors are acting out of fear or greed, two emotions that often drive market movements.

⸻

What the Extreme Fear vs. Extreme Greed Tool Is

The Fear and Greed Index ranges from 0 to 100 and reflects the overall mood of the market.
	•	0–24: Extreme Fear
	•	25–44: Fear
	•	45–55: Neutral
	•	56–75: Greed
	•	76–100: Extreme Greed

When the index moves toward 0, investors are very cautious and pessimistic.
When it moves toward 100, investors become overly confident and optimistic.

The concept behind the tool is simple: markets are driven by human psychology, not just fundamentals.

⸻

Extreme Fear

When the index shows Extreme Fear, it means investors are worried about losses. This often happens during:
	•	Market crashes
	•	Economic uncertainty
	•	Recession fears
	•	Major geopolitical events

During extreme fear:

📉 Investors sell stocks aggressively
💵 Money moves into safer assets like cash or bonds
📊 Stock prices often become undervalued

Many experienced investors believe extreme fear can create buying opportunities, because markets may be oversold.

A famous quote from Warren Buffett captures this idea:

“Be fearful when others are greedy and greedy when others are fearful.”

⸻

Extreme Greed

When the index shows Extreme Greed, investors are very optimistic and confident about the market.

This often happens during:
	•	Strong bull markets
	•	Rapid stock price increases
	•	High investor optimism
	•	Speculative bubbles

During extreme greed:

📈 Investors buy stocks aggressively
🚀 Risky assets become popular
💰 Valuations may become inflated

Extreme greed can sometimes signal that the market is overbought, meaning prices may be due for a correction.

⸻

What the Index Measures

The Fear and Greed Index uses seven different indicators to measure sentiment:
	1.	Stock Price Momentum – strength of market trends
	2.	Stock Price Strength – number of stocks hitting highs vs lows
	3.	Stock Price Breadth – overall participation in rallies
	4.	Put and Call Options – demand for protection vs speculation
	5.	Market Volatility – often measured by the CBOE Volatility Index
	6.	Safe Haven Demand – movement into bonds vs stocks
	7.	Junk Bond Demand – appetite for riskier debt

Together, these indicators provide a snapshot of market psychology.

⸻

How Investors Use It

Investors use the index as a contrarian indicator, meaning they often do the opposite of the crowd.

Examples:
	•	Extreme Fear → Possible buying opportunity
	•	Extreme Greed → Possible time to take profits

However, it should never be used alone. Professional investors combine it with:
	•	Fundamental analysis
	•	Economic data
	•	Technical indicators

⸻

Simple Example

Imagine the market drops sharply due to bad economic news.
	•	Investors panic
	•	Stocks sell off quickly
	•	The index falls to Extreme Fear

But if company fundamentals remain strong, long-term investors may see this as an opportunity to buy quality stocks at lower prices.

⸻

✅ In simple terms:
The Fear and Greed Index measures how emotional the market is, helping investors understand when markets might be overly pessimistic or overly optimistic.

In recent years, Amazon has periodically raised large amounts of capital by issuing corporate bonds to investors. A bond sale like this is essentially the company borrowing money from the public markets. Instead of taking out a traditional bank loan, Amazon sells bonds—debt securities that promise investors regular interest payments and repayment of the principal at a future date.

When Amazon conducts a bond sale, it typically works with major investment banks such as JPMorgan Chase, Goldman Sachs, and Morgan Stanley. These banks act as underwriters, helping structure the bonds, determine pricing, and sell them to institutional investors like pension funds, insurance companies, and mutual funds.

A typical Amazon bond offering is divided into multiple “tranches,” which are bonds with different maturities. For example, Amazon might issue bonds that mature in 3 years, 5 years, 10 years, or even 40 years. Each maturity has its own interest rate, known as the coupon. Shorter-term bonds usually offer lower yields, while longer-term bonds offer higher yields because investors are committing their money for a longer period of time.

Investors buy these bonds because Amazon is considered one of the safest corporate borrowers in the world. The company has a strong balance sheet, massive revenue from its e-commerce platform, cloud computing division Amazon Web Services, and diversified businesses including logistics, advertising, and streaming through Amazon Prime. Because of this financial strength, rating agencies such as Moody’s and S&P Global Ratings generally assign Amazon high credit ratings, which allows the company to borrow at relatively low interest rates.

One of the main reasons Amazon issues bonds—even though it generates tens of billions of dollars in cash flow—is financial flexibility. Bond financing allows the company to fund large strategic investments without immediately using its cash reserves. For instance, proceeds from bond sales may be used to expand data centers for AWS, build fulfillment warehouses, invest in artificial intelligence, acquire companies, or refinance existing debt at better rates.

Another reason is the current interest rate environment. If borrowing costs are relatively low, Amazon can lock in cheap long-term financing. This strategy became especially common after the monetary policies implemented by the Federal Reserve following the COVID-19 pandemic, which pushed interest rates lower and created strong demand for high-quality corporate bonds.

Demand for Amazon bonds is typically extremely strong. Large institutional investors view them as a stable investment that offers slightly higher yields than U.S. government debt issued by the U.S. Department of the Treasury. Because of this demand, Amazon’s bond offerings are often oversubscribed, meaning investors request more bonds than the company initially plans to issue.

From a broader market perspective, a major bond sale from a company as large as Amazon can signal confidence in credit markets and investor appetite for corporate debt. It also reflects how large technology companies increasingly use capital markets as a strategic financing tool rather than relying solely on equity or bank loans.

In summary, Amazon’s bond sales are large-scale borrowing events in which the company raises billions of dollars by issuing debt to investors. These offerings help finance long-term growth, maintain financial flexibility, and take advantage of favorable interest rates while providing investors with relatively safe, income-producing securities backed by one of the world’s most powerful companies.

A bond is essentially a loan made by an investor to a borrower. Instead of borrowing money from a bank, governments, municipalities, or companies borrow money from investors by issuing bonds.

When you buy a bond, you are lending money to the issuer for a specific period of time. In return, the issuer promises two things:
	1.	To pay regular interest payments, called the coupon.
	2.	To repay the original amount borrowed, called the principal or face value, when the bond reaches its maturity date.

For example, if a company issues a $1,000 bond with a 5% coupon rate and a 10-year maturity, the investor lends the company $1,000. The company then pays the investor 5% interest each year ($50). After 10 years, the company returns the original $1,000 along with the final interest payment.

Many bonds are issued by governments such as the U.S. Department of the Treasury, which sells Treasury bonds to help fund government spending. Corporations like Apple Inc. or Amazon also issue bonds to raise capital for investments, acquisitions, or expansion.

Bonds have several key features:

1. Face Value (Par Value)
The amount the issuer agrees to repay at maturity, often $1,000.

2. Coupon Rate
The fixed interest rate the bond pays to investors.

3. Maturity Date
The date when the bond issuer must repay the principal.

4. Yield
The actual return an investor earns if the bond is bought at a price different from its face value.

Bond prices can rise or fall in the market after they are issued. One major factor affecting bond prices is interest rates. When interest rates rise, existing bond prices usually fall because newer bonds offer higher yields. When rates fall, existing bonds become more valuable.

Investors often buy bonds because they are considered more stable than stocks and provide predictable income through interest payments. However, bonds still carry risks, such as interest rate risk, inflation risk, and credit risk if the issuer cannot repay the debt.

In simple terms, a bond is a structured IOU: investors lend money, earn interest over time, and get their original investment back when the bond matures. #investing #investingforbeginners #finance #stockmarket #bonds

The February 2026 Consumer Price Index (CPI) report, released by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, showed that inflation in the United States remained relatively stable but still slightly above the target set by the Federal Reserve. Overall, the data suggested that price pressures in the economy are cooling compared with previous years, yet inflation has not fully returned to the central bank’s long-term goal of 2 percent.

According to the report, headline CPI increased 0.3% month-over-month in February, following a 0.2% rise in January. On a year-over-year basis, inflation remained at 2.4%, unchanged from the previous month. This indicates that while prices are still rising, the pace of inflation has stabilized rather than accelerating.  

The core CPI, which excludes volatile food and energy prices and is closely watched by policymakers, rose 0.2% for the month and 2.5% over the past year. This reading was largely in line with economists’ expectations and suggested that underlying inflation pressures are slowly moderating.  

Several categories played key roles in February’s inflation data. Shelter costs remained the largest contributor to overall inflation, though the rate of increase slowed. Housing prices rose roughly 0.2% during the month and about 3% annually, indicating that rent growth and housing inflation are gradually cooling compared with earlier periods.  

Food prices continued to rise moderately, increasing 0.4% during February, while energy prices rose about 0.6%, driven mainly by gasoline and utility gas costs. At the same time, some categories helped offset inflation. Used vehicle prices declined, new car prices were largely unchanged, and auto insurance costs fell slightly, providing downward pressure on the overall index.  

While the February report appeared relatively calm, economists caution that the data reflects conditions before a major surge in oil prices linked to geopolitical tensions in the Middle East. Higher energy costs in March and beyond could push inflation higher in future reports if oil prices remain elevated.  

For financial markets, the report was interpreted as “steady but not fully cooled” inflation. Because inflation remains slightly above the Fed’s 2% target, policymakers are expected to remain cautious when considering interest-rate cuts. The data suggests the economy is moving toward price stability, but progress has slowed and inflation remains somewhat sticky.

In summary, the February CPI report showed stable inflation at 2.4%, modest monthly price growth, cooling housing inflation, and moderate increases in food and energy costs. While the report did not signal a resurgence of inflation, it confirmed that price pressures are still present and that the path back to the Federal Reserve’s target remains gradual.

subtitles: Did you know Google's first server was actually made out of Legos? Back in 1996, before Google was even a real company, Larry Page and Sergey Brin were two Stanford grad students trying to store a massive amount of data for an early version of their search engine. At the time, storage was incredible, incredibly expensive, kinda like how it is now. And proper server hardware was just out of reach for two grad students working on a research project. So instead of buying a real server rack, they built their own storage case using LEGO bricks. Mainly because Lego was cheap, sturdy, and easy to rebuild if they needed to expand more storage. So when they wanted to add another hard drive, they didn't need to replace the system, they just snapped on more bricks and expanded it. And that Lego server actually powered early Google. And it still exists today. It's on display at Stanford as the original Google server. a lot of people think the colourful Lego bricks are what inspired Google's logo, the blue, red, yellow and green, but it's actually never been confirmed. Windows 9 never existed….and the reason is one of the strangest stories in tech history. Microsoft skipped straight from Windows 8 to Windows 10, and many developers believe it’s because older software used lazy code that checked for operating systems starting with “Windows 9” to detect Windows 95 or Windows 98. If Microsoft had released Windows 9, thousands of legacy apps could have thought they were running on a 1990s system and broken instantly. It’s a wild example of how old software compatibility still shapes modern tech.

#windows10 #techgeek #windows #microsoft #techtok
subtitles: Why did Microsoft skip Windows 9? Well, back in the 90s we had Windows 95 and Windows 98. And a lot of programs back then were written in a super lazy way instead of properly checking the system version. Developers had written code that said if the name starts with Windows 9, it must be 95 or 98. Which worked back then. But imagine Microsoft launches something called Windows 9. Then thousands of old applications could look at it and be like oh cool, this is Windows 95 and then just switch it to ancient compatibility mode or just break now. Microsoft never officially said yeah, we skipped it because of that, but when they announced Windows 10 they said it was a big leap forward, a fresh start, and a new generation. But they're also really obsessed with backwards compatibility. Like they will do anything to keep old programs running. So avoiding a massive compatibility mess. Yeah, that would track. Was it 100% because of lazy programming? Probably not. But was it part of the reason? Pretty likely, but what story do you believe? Let me know in the comments.

I’m tired of two types of people.

The ones who, after any minor AI model update, scream “SWE IS SO OVER!!! YOU’RE DELUSIONAL IF YOU THINK OTHERWISE! THE END IS NEAR!!!” And the ones who always roll their eyes and proudly say “I never use AI” and shame anyone else who does.

Spoiler - they’re both wrong.

Don’t get me wrong, I use AI a lot on a daily basis, I like it, but I also see its advantages and disadvantages clearly.

Yeah, at some point AI will replace some programmers… the lazy ones. And it has nothing to do with AI’s capabilities. In today’s reality, you have to adapt, learn a lot, and master multiple things at the same time. If you can’t, if you don’t want to improve yourself, if you rely on AI only - REPLACED! Using Artificial Intelligence without Human Intelligence is a very bad idea 💀

And it’s equally stupid not to use it and deny how helpful it can be. Time is money, and AI can save you a lot of it. Denying such a powerful tool is just shooting yourself in the foot. I mean, if you already have a good technical knowledge, imagine how unstoppable you can be with AI by simply delegating a lot of things to it. Yeah, exactly.

So the point is: combine those two annoying types of people and find the balance. Use AI, but prompting alone won’t cut it - you still need good technical skills that allow you to understand what is going on and why.

Under something called the stepped up basis loophole, your heirs inherit that stock at its current value. The decades of gains wiped clean, never taxed, gone. This isn't a conspiracy theory. This is written into the tax code. It's called buy, borrow, die. And the people who use it aren't criminals. They're just working a different rule book than you were ever handed. Let that sit for a second. Now, I want to be clear. I'm not here to tell you the wealthy are evil. Some are, some aren't. That's not the point. The point is, this is their playbook, and now you know it. There are two tax systems in America. One runs on earned income, the sweat and clock kind. Wages, salaries, hourly work. The IRS sees every dollar before you do. The other runs on capital ownership, assets, investments. And capital is taxed at a lower rate, deferred, or in some cases, avoided entirely through generational wealth transfers. And the brutal irony, the person paying the highest effective tax rate in this country is often not the billionaire. It's the middle class worker, the nurse, the teacher, the truck driver. You grind the hardest, you keep the least. That's not an accident. That's architecture. Okay, here's where I refuse to leave you feeling hopeless. Because this isn't about doom. It's about awareness. And awareness is the first step to playing a smarter game. Here's the thing. The legal tools that the wealthy use to reduce their tax burden, most of them are available to you, too. They're just not advertised. No.1 tax advantaged accounts. Your 4 O 1 K, your IRA, your HSA. These are IRS approved Shields. Money you contribute to a traditional 4 O 1 K is not counted as taxable income in the year you earn it. In 2026, you can contribute up to $24,500 to your 4 O one K. You are legally deferring your tax Bill. Into the future. A Roth IRA flips it. You pay tax now, but every dollar it grows and every dollar you withdraw in retirement tax free forever. The 2026 contribution limit is 75 hundred dollars, and if you have a high deductible health plan, an HSA lets you contribute 4,400 dollars as an individual or 8,750 for a family. Triple tax advantaged, meaning your contributions go in tax free, grow tax free, and come out tax free for medical expenses. If you are not maxing these out, you are voluntarily paying more than you have to. No.2 capital gains awareness if you invest in index funds or etfs and hold them for one year or more, your gains are taxed at the long term capital gains rate, which in 2026 is 0% if you earn under $49,450. 15% for most middle income earners and 20% at the top. Compare that to the 22 to 37% you pay on ordinary income. The tax code literally rewards patience. No.3 side income and deductions if you run any kind of side business, a channel, freelance work, the small shop, you have access to business deductions that W2 employees simply don't. Home office equipment, software, mileage. These reduce your taxable income directly. The wealthy don't earn less, they report less, and they do it legally. Here's the deeper question. Underneath all of this, why doesn't anyone teach this? You spent 12 years in school, you Learned the Pythagorean theorem, you diagrammed sentences You memorized the dates of wars, but no one sat you down and said, here is how money is taxed. Here is how the system works. Here is what the wealthy know that you don't. That wasn't an oversight. Because a population that understands money is a population that makes different choices, different demands. That's uncomfortable for certain people in power. So they kept it complicated, they kept it boring. They made you feel like taxes were something that just happened to you, like weather. But taxes are not weather. They're policy. And policy can be understood. And once you understand it, you can work with it, around it, through it. You are not powerless here. You're just new to the game. And that changes today. The tax system was not designed to be your enemy, but it was also not designed to be your friend. It was designed for people who understood it, and those people have been winning quietly for decades. Now. You know the rules. You know about buy, borrow, die. You know about ordinary income versus capital gains. You know about Elon Musk paying zero dollars in taxes while you lost 30 cents on every dollar you earned. You know about the accounts, the 4:01 k, the Roth IRA, the HSA. But shield your money from the IRS before it ever gets taxed. The gap between the wealthy and everyone else isn't just about income. It's about financial literacy and the willingness to act on it. Start With one thing. Open that Roth IRA, max, your HSA. Hold that index fund for one more year. Every single move compounds. Every single dollar you protect from unnecessary taxation is a dollar that works for you, not the system. Because you've given them enough already. If this opened your eyes, don't let that feeling fade. You deserve to understand your money. And we're just getting started.

Using resources to compress decades of potential growth into a much shorter time frame. Now, let's be honest with ourselves. Most of us were never taught any of this. 10 Unsexy Habits That Save Me Thousands
#finance #money #fyp #tiktok #usa
subtitles: Three years ago, I was broke. Not struggling broke. I'm talking checking my bank account before buying a four dollar coffee and hoping the math worked out. And the worst part? I had a decent income, I just had absolutely nothing to show for it. No cushion, no savings. Just a number that never seemed to grow, no matter how hard I worked. What changed wasn't some app or a budgeting spreadsheet I'd abandoned in two weeks. It was 10 habits. 10 boring, unglamorous habits nobody puts on Instagram. And what surprised me most wasn't the money they saved. It was how fast they stopped feeling like effort. They just became who I was. I was 27, living in a city I couldn't afford. Convinced I was immune to financial advice because I'd read enough about it to sound educated. I knew about compound interest, I understood the 50 30 20 rule. And yet every Friday I found a reason to spend. I didn't start fixing this because I got motivated. I started because I was exhausted. Tired of that stomach dropping feeling every time I opened my banking app. Habit 1. I stopped buying things the moment I wanted them. When I see something I want, clothes, a gadget, a course, I add it to a list and wait 72 hours. 70% of the time I forget it exists entirely. Not because I force myself. The desire just evaporates on its own because the brain releases dopamine in anticipation. Of buying something, not in actually having it. The wanting always feels bigger than the owning. The other 30% of the time I still want it. And I buy it guilt free because I know it's real. This one habit saves me three to four thousand dollars a year on purchases I was seconds away from making. But two. I unsubscribe from every marketing email. This sounds small. It is not small. I was getting promotional emails from over 140 grams every single day. Sale ends tonight. Last chance. I wasn't consciously reading them, but they were quietly reshaping what I thought I needed. Unsubscribing took two hours one Sunday, one time forever. And eliminated an entire channel of manufactured desire I didn't know was running in the background. Habit 3. I started making coffee at home. Roll your eyes. I'll wait. Because this isn't about the coffee. It's about automatic spending. Automatic spending is a muscle. Every time you buy something without thinking, that muscle gets stronger. Making coffee at home was the first time I deliberately slowed down and made a different choice. That intentionality started spreading everywhere else. The coffee was just a first domino. Here's the part nobody talks about. The hardest part wasn't the habits. It was what I found underneath them. Because I hadn't just been spending money. I'd been using spending as a coping mechanism. Rough week at work? Buy something anxious? Buy something bored. On a Tuesday night? Scroll and buy something When I took that away, I had to sit with those feelings and for a while that was genuinely uncomfortable. Nobody tells you that fixing your finances is also an emotional project. I believe it's why most people fail. Not because the habits are hard, but because the habits hold up a mirror. Habit 4 I never grocery shop hungry. Research shows hungry shoppers spend up to 60% more. And not just on food, on everything. Hunger puts your brain into full acquisition mode. I've left stores with truffle oil, three types of cheese, and a bag of something I couldn't identify but felt compelled to buy. Ate none of it. Shop with a list. Shop full and you'll save 40 to 60 dollars every single trip without even trying. Habit 5 I do a subscription on it every six months, 20 minutes twice a year. Every time I do it, I find something. Last time a gym I hadn't visited in eight months, a meditation app I used twice, a cloud plan I was double paying for, and a software subscription I didn't even recognize it had been silently draining my account for over a year. Recurring charges are designed to be forgettable. The habit is simply to notice. Habit 6 I track my net worth once a month, not my spending. I tried detailed budgeting. I burned out in six weeks because it felt like financial prison. What worked was one number net worth assets minus liabilities. Once A month, 10 minutes. Watching that number slowly climb gave me momentum instead of shame. Progress builds habits. Shame doesn't. Somewhere around month four, something shifted. I had money in my account I hadn't spent, and instead of the usual stomach drop when I opened my banking app, I felt clear, steady. That quiet, unsexy feeling of having a cushion turned out to be more satisfying than anything I'd been buying to fill that gap. Habit 7 I pay myself first automatically. The moment a paycheck lands, a transfer fires to savings before I can see it, touch it, or talk myself out of it. It started at $50 a month. That's not the point. The point is that the behavior happens before my brain gets involved, before I can have a bad Thursday and decide I deserve a little treat. Willpower is a terrible financial strategy. It runs out, it has bad days. Automation doesn't. At 8, I Learned to say I can't afford that right now out loud without apology. Not I don't feel like it, not some vague excuse, just the plain, honest truth. This took me longer than any other habit because I'd absorbed the idea that admitting financial limits was embarrassing, that real adults could just do things, go places, say yes, the most financially solid people I know say this phrase constantly because they're not victims of their money. They're directing it somewhere intentional. Saying it out loud is its own form of Financial therapy. And the more you say it, the less it stings. Habit 9. I stopped upgrading things that still work. Phone works fine. Keep it. Car runs. Drive it. There's an entire industry worth hundreds of billions of dollars built around engineering. The anxiety that what you have is no longer enough. But the upgrade is almost never about the product. It's about the feeling of being current. My rule. I only upgrade when something breaks, not when something new comes out. In three years, this saved me more than almost anything else on this list. Habit 10. And this is the big one. I stopped using spending as a substitute for living. I told myself I was rewarding myself for working hard, and that's partially true. But most of my spending had nothing to do with enjoyment. It was about filling space. Weekends that felt hollow, evenings that felt purposeless. A restlessness I'd Learned I could quiet for 20 minutes by clicking buy now. When I stopped, I had to build a life that didn't need constant input to feel okay. More time with people, more time outside, more creating and less consuming. And here's what I found. That life cost almost nothing, and it feels better than anything I was buying to replace it. These habits will save you money, but what they're really doing is teaching you to stop running from yourself. So here they are. All 10. The 72 hour rule. Kill the marketing. E Mails make the coffee. Never shop hungry. Audit your subscriptions. Track net worth, not spending. Pay yourself first. Say you can't afford things. Stop upgrading what works. And stop filling your life with purchases instead of presents. None of these are glamorous, none of them will impress anyone. But a year from now, you'll open your banking app and feel something you haven't felt in a long time. Safe. And that feeling is worth more than anything I ever spent chasing it. If this hit differently than you expected, if it felt less like a money video and more like something you needed to hear, subscribe. I make honest, no fluff videos about building a life that works. Hit the bell. Drop a comment telling me which habit you're starting this week. I read every single one. See you in the next one.
